The ?? (null coalescing) operator is equivalent to isset() checks, so it silently treats undefined variables as null without emitting warnings or notices.
echo can take multiple comma-separated arguments, printing them in order without spaces.
print always returns 1, so it can be used within expressions, unlike echo which returns no value.
The ?: operator returns its left operand when it is truthy, and the right operand when it is falsy.
PHP 8 changed operator precedence so that arithmetic operators like + and - now bind more tightly than the concatenation operator '.'.
The ** operator is right-associative, so 2 ** 3 ** 2 evaluates as 2 ** (3 ** 2) = 2 ** 9 = 512.
Since PHP 8, the + operator has higher precedence than the concatenation operator, so it evaluates as 'sum: ' . (2 + 3).
Strict comparison (===) requires arrays to have the same key/value pairs in the same order with identical types, so different element ordering makes them unequal.
0 == false uses loose comparison (==), which converts types and returns true; strict comparison would use ===.

When compared with null, the other operand is cast to null, so null == 0, null == "", and null == false are all true.
Casting a string to int takes the leading numeric portion, so '42abc' becomes 42.
PHP converts the numeric string '5' to an integer, so the addition yields 10.
In PHP, casting false to string yields an empty string "", while true becomes "1".
Due to floating-point precision, 0.1 + 0.2 equals 0.30000000000000004, which is not identical to 0.3.
strrev() is not multibyte-safe; it reverses bytes, corrupting UTF-8 multibyte characters.
str_contains() checks if the needle 'world' appears in the haystack 'Hello world', which it does, so it returns true.
str_pad() can pad on the right (default), left, or both sides, depending on the optional STR_PAD_* argument.

In UTF-8, é is encoded as 2 bytes, so strlen() counts 5 characters as 6 bytes.
A negative start of -3 counts 3 characters from the end, so 'abcdef' from index 3 onward gives 'def'.
ucfirst() returns a new string; PHP strings are passed by value and never modified in place.
Heredoc syntax (<<<EOT) parses variables like double-quoted strings, while nowdoc syntax (<<<'EOT') treats the content literally without variable interpolation.
sort() reindexes the array with numeric keys starting at 0; asort() is the function that preserves key-value associations.
PHP automatically casts string keys containing valid integer strings (like '5') to the integer type when used as array keys.
in_array() uses loose (==) comparison by default; strict comparison is enabled only by passing true as the third parameter.
When called without a callback, array_filter() removes all entries whose values evaluate to false (like 0, '', null, [], '0').
By default, array_slice() reindexes numeric keys sequentially; you must pass true as the fourth parameter to preserve the original keys.
array_slice starts at index 1 and takes 2 elements: 20 and 30.
The union operator keeps all unique keys, with left-side values taking precedence, so the result has keys 'a' and 'b'.
PHP 8.1 added support for unpacking arrays with string keys using the spread operator.
In PHP 8, named arguments can be combined with spread unpacking, e.g. foo(...$args, named: 1).
In PHP, anonymous functions do not inherit outer scope variables unless explicitly imported via the use keyword or arrow functions (fn) which auto-capture by value.
func_num_args() returns the number of arguments actually passed to the function, regardless of declared parameters.
PHP arrow functions (fn) can only contain a single expression, and using curly braces or multiple statements is a parse error.
Arrow functions automatically capture outer variables by value (at definition time), unlike closures which require explicit 'use (&$var)' for references.
A static closure cannot be bound to an object instance, so $this is not automatically captured inside it.
The closure captured $x by value at creation time, so later changes to $x don't affect it.
In weak (coercive) typing mode, the string "5" is a numeric string and is automatically coerced to the int 5.
Constructor property promotion was introduced in PHP 8.0, allowing properties to be declared directly in constructor parameters.
Declaring a method as final prevents subclasses from overriding it.
The final keyword prevents a method from being overridden by child classes.
Private properties are only accessible within the class that declares them; subclasses must use protected or public visibility instead.
An anonymous class gets a generated name like 'class@anonymous/path/to/file.php:1$0'; stripping the path yields 'class@anonymous'.
Private parent methods are not inherited or part of the child's API, so a child class can freely declare a method with the same name and any visibility without conflict.
__get() is called when a property is inaccessible (non-existent OR private/protected from outside scope), not only when it does not exist.
Modifying a readonly property after initialization throws an instance of the Error class, not Exception.
PHP interfaces may declare constants, which are inherited by classes implementing the interface.
The instanceof operator checks whether an object is an instance of a specified class or interface.
Since PHP 5.3, interfaces may declare public static methods that implementing classes must define.

In PHP, interface methods cannot contain a body or default implementation; only traits and classes can provide method implementations.
Abstract methods in PHP abstract classes may be declared public, protected, or (since PHP 7.1) private visibility.
cases() returns an array of all defined cases, and Foo defines three: A, B, and C.
Since PHP 8.2, traits can declare constants, which are then available in the classes that use the trait.
In PHP 7+, both Exception and Error implement the Throwable interface, making it their common ancestor.
TypeError extends the Error class, and Error and Exception are separate hierarchies (both implement Throwable), so a catch (Exception) block does not catch TypeError.
The @ operator only suppresses errors and warnings; exceptions must be caught with try/catch and cannot be silenced.
intdiv() throws DivisionByZeroError when the divisor is zero.
The finally block executes whether or not an exception was thrown and whether or not it was caught.
An exception thrown inside a finally block overrides the try block's return value or pending exception and propagates instead.
Any object, including an Exception instance, casts to boolean true.
Shutdown functions registered with register_shutdown_function() are executed when script execution stops, including when exit() or die() is called.
The use statement only creates an alias for the class name; the class file is loaded only when the class is actually used (e.g., instantiated), typically via an autoloader.
In PHP, `use function` imports a function while `use const` imports a constant.
PSR-4 replaces the 'App\' prefix with 'src/', so the remaining namespace path maps directly to directories: Controller/Api/UserController.php.
Composer's vendor/autoload.php registers its autoloader functions (class loader and others) using spl_autoload_register().
The __NAMESPACE__ magic constant returns a string with the name of the current namespace (empty string in global scope).
An unqualified class name in `new` is resolved relative to the current namespace (with import rules applied), not from the global root; only a leading `\` refers to the global root.
PSR-4 replaces the namespace prefix App\ with src/, so App\Model\User maps to src/Model/User.php.
Use statements may only appear at the top level of a file or namespace; they cannot be placed inside a function body.
In PHP, arrays are assigned by value (with copy-on-write optimization) unless explicitly passed by reference with &.
PHP arrays are copied by value, so appending to $b does not affect $a, which still has 2 elements.
PHP functions have their own scope, so global variables are only accessible via the global keyword, $GLOBALS array, or parameters.
Unsetting $GLOBALS['x'] removes the global variable itself entirely, not just within the current function.
The parameter is passed by reference (&$x), so incrementing $x inside the function modifies $n directly, making it 6.
When iterating by value, foreach operates on a copy (or snapshot) of the array, so modifications made inside the loop do not affect the iteration of the current pass.
A static property belongs to the class itself, so it is shared by all instances and changes are visible in every object.
PHP casts boolean array keys to integers, so true becomes key 1.
Since PHP 7, a generator may return a value with return, retrievable only after the generator finishes via its getReturn() method.
A generator cannot be rewound once iteration has started; calling rewind() after it has begun iteration throws an exception, so a generator can only be traversed once.
In PHP, `yield from` delegates iteration to another generator, Traversable object, or array.
A function containing yield returns a Generator object, so get_class() returns the class name 'Generator'.
The generator yields 1, 2, and 3 via `yield from`, so `iterator_to_array` produces an array of 3 elements.
SplStack implements a LIFO (last-in-first-out) stack, not a FIFO queue; SplQueue is the FIFO structure.
ArrayIterator wraps an array or object and lets you traverse it using the Iterator interface methods.
ArrayObject implements IteratorAggregate, so foreach works on it via getIterator().
password_hash() automatically generates and includes a cryptographically secure salt in the returned hash, so providing one separately is unnecessary (and the salt option is deprecated).
PASSWORD_DEFAULT currently uses bcrypt (via password_hash) with an automatic salt, not md5.
password_verify() returns true because the hash was generated from the same password 'secret'.
strip_tags() only removes HTML and PHP tags from a string; SQL injection is prevented with prepared statements or functions like proper escaping/quoting.
Calling session_regenerate_id() upon login replaces the session ID, preventing attackers from using a known fixed session ID to hijack the authenticated session.
php_sapi_name() returns a string with the name of the Server API, such as 'cli' or 'fpm-fcgi'.
session_destroy() removes server-side session data; the client cookie remains and must be removed separately, e.g. with setcookie().
Session data is only loaded into the $_SESSION superglobal after session_start() is called (or automatic session start is enabled).
The array_find() function was introduced in PHP 8.4 as part of new array search functions.
Property hooks (get/set defined directly in property declarations) were introduced in PHP 8.4.
PHP 8.4 introduced asymmetric visibility with the public private(set) syntax for read/write access control.
The #[\NoDiscard] attribute was introduced in PHP 8.5 to mark functions whose return values should not be ignored.
The pipe operator |> was introduced in PHP 8.5, allowing the result of one expression to be passed as a single argument to another function.
The clone-with syntax (clone($obj, ['prop' => value])) was introduced in PHP 8.4.
array_first() and array_last() were added in PHP 8.5 via an RFC.
The Partial Function Application v2 RFC was adopted for PHP 8.5.
The clamp_v2 RFC, which introduced the clamp() function, was implemented in PHP 8.4.
The Context Managers RFC is not adopted; it has not passed the voting/implementation stage to become part of PHP.
The Bound-Erased Generic Types (generics) RFC for PHP was ultimately declined in 2026.
No RFC has been accepted to make PHP thread-safe (ZTS) by default; ZTS remains optional and non-default as of November 2026.
PHP 8.5 (released November 2025) still has no generics/parameterized types support.
PHP 8.5 was released in November 2025 and is the latest stable version, while PHP 8.6 is scheduled for GA on 2026-11-19 and has not been released as of 2026-11-07.
The PHP 6 project was abandoned and the next major release after 5.6 was PHP 7.0 in 2015, so PHP 6 never shipped.
The #[\Deprecated] attribute RFC was accepted and implemented in PHP 8.4, allowing core functions to mark deprecated usage.
In clean/onion architecture, dependencies only point inward, so inner layers have no knowledge of outer layers.
Domain entities should be pure, framework-agnostic PHP classes depending only on the language and standard library, with persistence concerns handled elsewhere.
Controllers and Twig templates are part of the presentation/framework layer; business logic belongs in the domain/application layer where use cases themselves live.
In onion architecture, the domain model (entities) sits at the very center, with layers like domain services, application services, and infrastructure wrapped around it.
Tools like deptrac analyze dependencies between layers and fail the build when forbidden calls are detected.
A use case should depend on plain input data (e.g., DTOs/arrays) and abstractions, not on framework-specific objects like HTTP requests or an EntityManager, to remain decoupled and testable.
A Repository provides a collection-like interface over aggregates/entities while encapsulating the underlying storage mechanism.

In clean architecture, infrastructure details like the database live in the outer layer behind interfaces, so the domain and use case layers remain unchanged when swapping PostgreSQL for another database.
In DDD, an aggregate is a cluster of domain objects treated as a single consistency unit with a root entity, not merely a database table.
Value Objects are defined by their attribute values, are immutable, and equality is based on those values rather than object identity.
In Domain-Driven Design, the aggregate root is the single external entry point of an aggregate through which all changes and accesses must pass.
In Domain-Driven Design, repositories are defined per aggregate root, since aggregates are accessed as whole units rather than through their internal entities.
Ubiquitous language, a core Domain-Driven Design concept, is the shared vocabulary used by both developers and domain experts to describe the model.
In Domain-Driven Design, a bounded context is the boundary within which a model and its ubiquitous language are consistent, while the same terms outside may refer to different models.
DDD recommends rich domain models where behavior and business logic live inside the entities, not anemic models with logic pushed into services.
In Domain-Driven Design, a bounded context defines the boundaries within which a particular model applies, so the same concept is represented by a different class in each context.

Symfony's DI container instantiates services lazily, constructing them only when they are first requested, unless configured otherwise (e.g., synthetic services or eager instantiation via compiler passes).
The Symfony console command `php bin/console debug:router` lists all registered routes.
Symfony autowiring automatically registers and injects services based on type hints, so manual declaration of every service in services.yaml is not required.
Twig compiles templates into PHP classes and caches them so they are reused between requests.
In dev, Symfony tracks container resources (config files, classes, etc.) and only recompiles the DI container when one of them changes, otherwise it reuses the cached container.
Symfony uses the APP_ENV environment variable (defined in .env) to select the active environment such as dev or prod.
Symfony's controller resolver invokes the method externally, so routed controller methods must be public.
Subscribers and listeners are treated the same way at dispatch time; execution order depends on registered priority (and registration order), not on using the SubscriberInterface.
Symfony 6.0 removed the deprecated Guard authenticator system in favor of authenticators implementing AuthenticatorInterface, introduced in the new authentication system.
The #[IsGranted] attribute on a controller method checks a role/permission and throws a 403 AccessDeniedException if not satisfied.
Symfony security voters are the mechanism used with $security->isGranted('EDIT', $post) to decide access to a specific object.
Symfony 7 dropped support for doctrine annotations, so validation constraints must be declared as PHP attributes.
Symfony forms enable CSRF protection by default, automatically adding and validating a CSRF token field on submission.
Symfony validation is always performed server-side; HTML5 client-side validation is only a convenience and cannot be trusted.
Symfony MakerBundle's `make:form` command generates a form class (FormType).
Symfony erases the password from the serialized security token before storing it in the session, keeping only the roles, username, and other non-sensitive data.
In Symfony 4+, bundle configuration is stored in the config/packages directory, typically with one configuration file per bundle or topic.
This is the Symfony convention: .env is committed with safe defaults while real secrets go into the git-ignored .env.local.
The `php bin/console debug:container` command lists all registered services and aliases in the dependency injection container.
The compiled service container is frozen at runtime, so calling setParameter() from a controller throws a LogicException instead of changing the parameter.
Since Symfony 4.0, services are private by default (public: false) and can only be injected via autowiring or the service container's compiler, not fetched directly from the container.
Bundles work with sensible defaults; configuration in config/packages is optional and only needed to override defaults.
In Symfony, environment variables are accessed in services.yaml using the %env(VAR)% syntax.
Symfony uses the APP_DEBUG environment variable to enable debug mode, which activates the profiler and Twig debugging.
Symfony Messenger supports multiple handlers per message; all registered handlers will be called.
The sync transport handles the message immediately in the same process, bypassing the queue entirely.
The Symfony console command `php bin/console messenger:consume` starts the worker that processes messages from the Messenger transports (queues).
In Symfony Messenger, retry_strategy is configured per transport inside the messenger.transports section, allowing each transport its own retry configuration.
Symfony Messenger's default serializer is PhpSerializer using PHP's serialize() format; JSON serialization requires configuring a Serializer with the 'json' format.
The Symfony Scheduler component creates scheduled messages (Schedules) which are then dispatched and handled via the Messenger component.
The Messenger 'doctrine' transport persists queued messages in database tables (messenger_messages) managed by Doctrine.
Symfony Messenger's middleware stack is configurable, allowing custom middleware to be added before or after the built-in middleware.
Symfony follows a fixed schedule: new major versions every two years and minor versions every six months, in May and November.
Following Symfony's release policy of raising the minimum PHP version with each major release (7.0 requires PHP 8.2), Symfony 8 requires PHP 8.3.
Symfony 7.0 removed support for docblock annotations, requiring PHP attributes instead for validation, routes, and other configuration.
Symfony's AssetMapper component serves and versions CSS/JS files directly (using importmap.php for JS imports) without requiring Node.js, npm, or webpack.
Symfony 6.4 is an LTS (Long-Term Support) release, supported with bug fixes and security patches for extended periods.
Major Symfony releases are exactly where deprecated features from the previous branch are removed.
Symfony publishes an UPGRADE document with every major release describing all changes and how to migrate.
The AssetMapper component (symfony/asset-mapper, part of the Asset ecosystem) manages JavaScript/CSS assets and import maps without needing Node.js or Webpack.
Symfony 8.2 is scheduled for release in late November 2026, so as of November 7, 2026 it has not been released yet.
Following Symfony's regular six-month release cycle, version 8.2 is scheduled for release in November 2026, following 8.1 in May 2026 and 8.0 in November 2025.
Symfony minor versions increment by one, so the release following 8.1 is 8.2.
In Symfony only x.0 versions are major releases; x.2 releases are minor releases that maintain backward compatibility, and Symfony 8.2 does not require rewriting applications.

PHP's backward compatibility guarantee applies to minor releases within a major version, so moving from 8.1 to 8.2 should not break existing code (excluding deprecated features being removed at major versions).
Following Symfony's release pattern (e.g., 6.4 before 7.0 and 7.4 before 8.0), the last minor release of the 8.x branch is 8.4, right before 9.0.
Symfony 8.x raises the minimum to PHP 8.2 (following Symfony's policy of requiring the oldest still-supported PHP branch), so PHP 8.5 would not be required.
Symfony guarantees backwards compatibility within a major release, so any feature deprecated during the 8.x minor releases will only be removed in Symfony 9.0.
Twig templates can only call registered filters, functions, and methods exposed by the Twig environment, not arbitrary PHP code.
Twig enables auto-escaping with the 'html' strategy by default, so printed variables are escaped unless autoescape is disabled.
The Twig |e filter escapes a string for safe output, defaulting to the HTML context (other strategies like js or css can be specified).
The intl-extra package provides the format_number filter (backed by PHP's intl NumberFormatter) to format numbers per locale.
The raw filter marks a value as safe so Twig's auto-escaping is skipped for it.
In Twig, {{ }} outputs expression values, while {% %} executes statements like if conditions, for loops, and set assignments.
Twig allows declaring variables inside templates using the {% set %} tag.
The Twig dump() function outputs the debug structure of a variable, similar to var_dump(), when the debug mode is enabled.
Bootstrap is a front-end CSS/JS library of prebuilt UI components like grids and modals, whereas SPA frameworks (React, Angular, Vue) manage application state and routing.
The .container class is responsive and has a fixed max-width that changes at each breakpoint, unlike .container-fluid which spans full width.
The Bootstrap grid splits each row into 12 columns, not 16.
The list sm, md, lg, xl, xxl actually contains six breakpoints, not five (five would exclude xxl).
In Bootstrap, spacing utilities like .mt-3 or .px-2 are generated from a scale where each step is a multiple of the $spacer variable (default 1rem).
In Bootstrap 5, interactive components are enabled with data attributes prefixed with data-bs-, such as data-bs-toggle="dropdown".
Bootstrap 5 removed the jQuery dependency and all its components work with plain vanilla JavaScript.
Bootstrap dark mode is enabled with the data-bs-theme="dark" attribute on the root element, not a .dark class.
Doctrine ORM does not create tables automatically at runtime; you must generate the schema explicitly using tools like the SchemaTool or Doctrine Migrations.
EntityManager::persist() schedules a new entity for insertion, making it managed, and the actual INSERT SQL is deferred until flush() is called.
Doctrine ORM 3 removed EntityManager::merge() entirely; merging is no longer supported, so the method neither exists nor can make an object managed.
DQL (Doctrine Query Language) operates on entities and their fields, which Doctrine translates into SQL over tables and columns.
In Doctrine, Repository::find() returns null when no entity matching the given id exists.
DoctrineBundle does not automatically call flush(); you must call it explicitly on the entity manager to persist changes.
Once an entity is managed (e.g., fetched via find()), Doctrine's Unit of Work detects changes at flush() time, so no additional persist() call is needed to commit modifications.
remove() only schedules the entity for deletion; the DELETE query is actually executed when flush() is called.
MVCC allows readers and writers to work concurrently, so readers do not block writers and writers do not block readers.
The EXPLAIN command shows a query's execution plan without actually executing the query.

SERIAL is a legacy convenience (an auto-incrementing BIGINT with different column semantics, ownership, and permissions) while GENERATED ... AS IDENTITY is the SQL-standard identity column mechanism, so they differ in behavior and are not just aliases for each other.
PostgreSQL follows the SQL standard and treats NULLs as distinct, so a UNIQUE constraint allows multiple rows with NULL in the column.
PostgreSQL's string_agg(value, separator) aggregate function concatenates strings with a delimiter.
Plain VACUUM marks dead tuple space as reusable within the table files but does not shrink them; only VACUUM FULL returns space to the operating system.
In a window function's OVER clause, PARTITION BY divides rows into groups the function is computed over independently.
READ COMMITTED only prevents dirty reads; non-repeatable reads are only prevented at the REPEATABLE READ isolation level or higher.
PostgreSQL executes each standalone statement in its own implicit transaction (autocommit) unless an explicit transaction is started with BEGIN.
The COMMIT command ends a transaction and permanently saves all its changes.
Indexes help any query with a WHERE clause on the indexed column, including UPDATE and DELETE statements, not just SELECTs.
PostgreSQL supports SAVEPOINT to mark points within a transaction that can be rolled back to with ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT, without aborting the whole transaction.
EXPLAIN ANALYZE actually executes the query and reports real timing; only plain EXPLAIN shows the plan without running it.
The pgvector extension provides vector data types and similarity-search indexes for embedding search in PostgreSQL.
A partial index only includes and indexes rows that satisfy the WHERE condition, making it smaller and faster for queries that match that condition.

PostgreSQL implements SERIALIZABLE using Serializable Snapshot Isolation (SSI), which relies on snapshot isolation plus predicate-based lock monitoring for dangerous read-write patterns, not by locking the rows a transaction reads.
HTTP 201 is the 'Created' status code, indicating the request successfully resulted in a new resource being created.
HTTP status 204 (No Content) indicates a successful request with an empty response body, commonly used after DELETE operations.
Per the HTTP specification, DELETE is idempotent: repeating the request on the same resource leaves the end state unchanged (the resource remains deleted).
Access-Control-Allow-Origin is sent by the server, not the client, to indicate which origins are permitted to access its resources.
HTTP 429 Too Many Requests is the standard status code indicating the client has sent too many requests in a given time and exceeded a rate limit.
It's the opposite: 4xx codes indicate client errors and 5xx codes indicate server-side errors.
The Content-Type header specifies the MIME type of the body of the request or response.
RFC 5789 defines PATCH as non-idempotent-safe, while PUT is required to be idempotent.
Plain == comparison is not timing-safe and doesn't handle algorithm/rehashing logic, so password_verify() (or hash_equals()) should be used instead.
CSRF tokens are generated server-side, stored in the session, embedded in forms, and validated on the server for unsafe requests like POST.
The CSP policy is delivered via the Content-Security-Policy HTTP response header.
OAuth 2.0 is an authorization framework; an access token grants permissions but does not identify the user — that's what OpenID Connect adds.
XSS is prevented by escaping output (e.g., htmlspecialchars when rendering), not merely by validating input before database storage.
The authorization server returns an authorization 'code' parameter to the redirect_uri, which the client then exchanges for an access token.
Refresh tokens are long-lived credentials used to request new access tokens without requiring the user to re-authenticate.
A salt does not need to be secret—it is typically stored alongside the hash and is required for verification; its purpose is to prevent precomputed rainbow-table attacks.
PHPUnit only recognizes and runs test methods in classes that extend TestCase.
setUp() runs before each individual test method; setUpBeforeClass() is the method that runs once before all tests in the class.
A data provider can supply multiple sets of arguments, causing the test to run once for each set.
PHPUnit's expectException($class) method declares that the tested code is expected to throw an exception of the given class.
It's the opposite: stubs simply return predefined data, while mocks verify which methods were called with what arguments.
PHPUnit 10 introduced structured metadata attributes like #[DataProvider], and the old @dataProvider annotation is deprecated in favor of them.
PHPUnit supports test dependencies via the @depends annotation, allowing a test to receive the return value of a test it depends on.
PHPUnit runs tests in random order when you pass the --order-by=random command-line option.
